prompt: Text can be written between single quotes or between double quotes. How do the two differ?
optionA: Single quotes hold text and double quotes hold formatted text
optionB: Only in which quote character they can contain without escaping
optionC: Double quotes allow longer text
optionD: Single quotes are faster to process
correctAnswerText: Only in which quote character they can contain without escaping
explanation: The two produce identical text. Which one is chosen matters only when the text itself contains a quote.

prompt: Which of these is a valid way to write text?
optionA: Opening with a single quote and closing with a double
optionB: Opening with a double quote and closing with a single
optionC: Opening and closing with no quote at all
optionD: Opening and closing with the same quote character
correctAnswerText: Opening and closing with the same quote character
explanation: The closing quote has to match the opening one. Mismatched quotes leave the literal unterminated.

prompt: Two pieces of text are written identically except that one uses single quotes and the other double. Are the resulting values the same?
optionA: Yes; the quote form is not part of the text
optionB: No; the quote characters are included in the value
optionC: No; one is longer than the other
optionD: Only if the text contains no letters
correctAnswerText: Yes; the quote form is not part of the text
explanation: Quotes mark where the text begins and ends and do not become part of it. The two values compare equal.

prompt: What decides which quote form to use for a piece of text?
optionA: The length of the text
optionB: Whether the text contains numbers
optionC: What quote characters the text itself contains
optionD: Personal preference alone, in every case
correctAnswerText: What quote characters the text itself contains
explanation: Choosing the form the text does not contain avoids escaping altogether. Where the text contains neither, preference genuinely does decide.

prompt: A piece of text contains both a single quote and a double quote. What follows about writing it with ordinary quotes?
optionA: It cannot be written at all
optionB: Whichever form is chosen, one of the two characters will need escaping
optionC: It must be split into two separate pieces
optionD: Single quotes will work without escaping
correctAnswerText: Whichever form is chosen, one of the two characters will need escaping
explanation: Containing both removes the option of picking the form the text avoids. A triple-quoted form is the other way out.

prompt: A backslash followed by the letter n appears inside a piece of text. What does that pair produce?
optionA: The two characters, a backslash and an n
optionB: A backslash only
optionC: An instruction that is removed with no character produced
optionD: A single line break character
correctAnswerText: A single line break character
explanation: The pair stands together for one character that is neither of the two written. That is the whole purpose of an escape.

prompt: How many characters does an escape sequence of a backslash and one letter produce?
optionA: One
optionB: Two
optionC: None
optionD: It depends on the letter
correctAnswerText: One
explanation: One character results, though two were written: the written form and the value differ in length.

prompt: How is a literal backslash written inside ordinary text?
optionA: As one backslash
optionB: As a backslash followed by a space
optionC: As two backslashes
optionD: A backslash cannot appear in text
correctAnswerText: As two backslashes
explanation: A single backslash begins an escape, so producing one requires escaping the backslash itself. The written form is twice the length of the result.

prompt: A student writes text containing a backslash and one letter, expecting to see both characters, and something else appears. What has happened?
optionA: The backslash was removed and the letter kept
optionB: The pair was read as an escape sequence and produced a different single character
optionC: The text was truncated at the backslash
optionD: The letter was removed and the backslash kept
correctAnswerText: The pair was read as an escape sequence and produced a different single character
explanation: Only some letters form an escape, which is why this surprises people unevenly. Doubling the backslash produces the two characters intended.

prompt: Two literals are written identically except that one carries a marker before its opening quote indicating interpolation. Both contain braces around a name. What differs?
optionA: Nothing; braces always interpolate
optionB: The unmarked one produces an error
optionC: The marked one is longer
optionD: The marked one replaces the braced section with a value; the unmarked one contains the braces as text
correctAnswerText: The marked one replaces the braced section with a value; the unmarked one contains the braces as text
explanation: Interpolation happens only when the literal is marked for it. Without the marker the braces are ordinary characters.

prompt: An unmarked literal contains braces around the word total. What does it produce?
optionA: The braces and the word total, as written
optionB: The value of a variable called total
optionC: An error, since total is not defined
optionD: An empty piece of text
correctAnswerText: The braces and the word total, as written
explanation: Without the interpolation marker nothing is substituted. The braces are characters like any others.

prompt: What makes a literal interpolate the values named inside it?
optionA: The presence of braces
optionB: The names inside being defined
optionC: A marker on the literal itself
optionD: The literal being assigned to a variable
correctAnswerText: A marker on the literal itself
explanation: The marker is what turns braces into substitution points. Defined names and braces alone change nothing.

prompt: A developer builds a message by joining two literals together with an operator, and the second literal is marked for interpolation while the first is not. What happens to braces in the first?
optionA: They interpolate, since the two are joined
optionB: They remain as literal braces, since the marker applies to one literal only
optionC: The join fails because the two forms differ
optionD: They are removed from the result
correctAnswerText: They remain as literal braces, since the marker applies to one literal only
explanation: Marking is a property of each literal rather than of the expression. Joining them does not spread the marker.

prompt: A name holds the value 7. An interpolating literal reads: Total: followed by braces around that name. What text is produced?
optionA: Total: name
optionB: Total: {7}
optionC: Total: "7"
optionD: Total: 7
correctAnswerText: Total: 7
explanation: The braced section is replaced by the value written out, and the surrounding text is kept. No quotes are added around a number.

prompt: A name holds a piece of text that was written between quotes in the source. When that name is substituted into an interpolating literal, does the output show the quotes?
optionA: No; the quotes marked where the text began and ended and were never part of it
optionB: Yes; text values are always written out with their quotes
optionC: Yes, but single quotes only
optionD: Only when the text contains a space
correctAnswerText: No; the quotes marked where the text began and ended and were never part of it
explanation: Quotes delimit a literal in the source and do not survive into the value. Substitution writes out what the value holds, which never included them.

prompt: A literal is marked raw. What does that change?
optionA: The text is displayed differently
optionB: The text cannot be changed afterwards
optionC: Backslashes are kept as backslashes rather than beginning escape sequences
optionD: Interpolation is disabled
correctAnswerText: Backslashes are kept as backslashes rather than beginning escape sequences
explanation: A raw literal changes what the written characters mean and not how the result is used. Every backslash stands for itself.

prompt: A Windows-style path with single backslashes is written as an ordinary literal and again as a raw one. How do the two results differ?
optionA: They are identical, since paths contain no escapes
optionB: The ordinary one has some backslash pairs converted to other characters; the raw one is as written
optionC: The raw one has its backslashes doubled
optionD: The ordinary one removes the backslashes entirely
correctAnswerText: The ordinary one has some backslash pairs converted to other characters; the raw one is as written
explanation: Only the pairs that form escapes are converted, so the ordinary literal is right in some places and wrong in others. That unevenness is what makes the fault confusing.

prompt: A triple-quoted literal spans three lines of text. What does it contain?
optionA: The three lines joined with spaces
optionB: The first line only
optionC: The three lines with the breaks removed
optionD: The three lines including the line breaks between them
correctAnswerText: The three lines including the line breaks between them
explanation: Line breaks inside a triple-quoted literal are part of the text. That is the reason for using the form.

prompt: A triple-quoted literal opens, then a line break, then the word Hello. What does the value begin with?
optionA: A line break, before the word Hello
optionB: The word Hello, with the break discarded
optionC: A space, then the word Hello
optionD: Nothing; the literal is empty until the second line
correctAnswerText: A line break, before the word Hello
explanation: The break immediately after the opening quotes is inside the literal like any other. Ending the first line with a backslash is the usual way to suppress it.

prompt: A triple-quoted literal is written inside an indented function, so every line after the first begins with eight spaces of indentation. A triple-quoted literal keeps every character between its quotes, including leading spaces. What does the value contain?
optionA: No leading spaces, since indentation is stripped
optionB: Eight spaces on the first line only
optionC: Eight spaces at the start of each of those lines
optionD: A single space at the start of each line
correctAnswerText: Eight spaces at the start of each of those lines
explanation: The indentation that makes the code readable becomes part of the text. Output that is mysteriously shifted to the right is the usual symptom.

prompt: A value of 3.14159 is placed into a literal with a format asking for two decimal places. What text appears?
explanation: The format controls how many decimal places are written out. The remaining digits are not shown.

prompt: Two values, 2.567 and 2.561, are each written out with a format asking for two decimal places. What do the two produce?
explanation: A precision rounds rather than cutting digits off, so the two go in different directions and give 2.57 and 2.56. Truncating both would have produced the same pair of digits twice.

prompt: A value of 12 is placed into a literal with a format asking for a width of five. A width pads a value that is shorter than the width and does not shorten one that is longer. What text appears?
optionA: The digits 12 padded out to five characters
optionB: The digits 12, unchanged
optionC: The digits 12 truncated to fit
optionD: Five copies of the digits 12
correctAnswerText: The digits 12 padded out to five characters
explanation: A width states a minimum rather than a maximum. A value longer than the width is written out in full.

prompt: The text "ab" is added to the text "cd". What is produced?
optionA: ab cd
optionB: The two kept separate
optionC: abcd
optionD: An error
correctAnswerText: abcd
explanation: Adding text joins the two with nothing between them. No separator is inserted.

prompt: The text "12" is added to the text "3". What is produced?
optionC: "12" and "3" as separate values
optionD: An error
explanation: Both operands are text, so they are joined rather than summed. Looking like numbers changes nothing about what they are.

prompt: A program reads two values typed by a user and adds them, producing 57 where 12 was expected. Values read from a user arrive as text, and adding text joins it rather than summing it. What were the two values?
optionA: 50 and 7, summed correctly
optionB: 5 and 7, summed incorrectly by the language
optionC: 57 and 0, entered as one value
optionD: 5 and 7, arriving as text and joined rather than summed
correctAnswerText: 5 and 7, arriving as text and joined rather than summed
explanation: Joining "5" and "7" gives "57", which is exactly what was seen. Converting each to a number before adding is the fix.

prompt: Two quoted pieces of text are written next to each other with nothing between them. What results?
optionA: One piece of text, being the two joined
optionB: Two separate pieces of text
optionC: An error, since no operator was given
optionD: The first piece only
correctAnswerText: One piece of text, being the two joined
explanation: Adjacent literals join automatically with no operator needed. This is deliberate and useful for splitting a long piece of text across lines.

prompt: A long message is written across three lines as three adjacent quoted pieces, each ending in a space. What results?
optionA: Three separate messages
optionB: One message with no spaces between the parts
optionC: One message with a space between each part
optionD: One message with a line break between the parts
correctAnswerText: One message with a space between each part
explanation: The pieces join exactly as written, so the trailing spaces survive and the line breaks in the source do not. Forgetting those spaces is how words run together.

prompt: A list is written with four quoted items and a comma is accidentally omitted between the second and third. Two quoted pieces with nothing between them join into one, and no comma separates the second and third items. How many items does the list hold?
optionA: Four, since all four are still written
optionB: Three, with the second and third joined into one
optionC: Two, since the missing comma splits the list
optionD: None; the list is invalid
correctAnswerText: Three, with the second and third joined into one
explanation: The join is silent and produces a perfectly valid list one item shorter than intended. Nothing reports an error, which is what makes this hard to spot.

prompt: A name holds a list of three numbers. It is placed into an interpolating literal. What appears?
optionA: The three numbers with spaces between them
optionB: The number of items in the list
optionC: An error, since a list is not text
optionD: The list written out, including its brackets and separators
correctAnswerText: The list written out, including its brackets and separators
explanation: Any value is written out in its usual form when substituted. The brackets are part of how a list is written.

prompt: A name holds the value representing absence of a value. It is placed into an interpolating literal. What appears?
optionA: The word that names that absence, written out as text
optionB: Nothing, leaving a gap
optionC: An empty pair of braces
optionD: An error, since there is no value to write
correctAnswerText: The word that names that absence, written out as text
explanation: The absence is itself a value with a written form, so it appears as a word in the output. A report reading "Owner: None" is the usual and confusing symptom.

prompt: A report is generated for every record and one field is sometimes unset. The output for those records reads oddly, with a word appearing where a name should be. Substituting an unset value writes out the word naming that absence rather than producing nothing. What is happening?
optionA: The field is being read from the wrong record
optionB: The literal is missing its interpolation marker
optionC: The unset value is being written out as a word rather than leaving a blank
optionD: The report is truncating the field
correctAnswerText: The unset value is being written out as a word rather than leaving a blank
explanation: Nothing fails, so every record generates a report and some of them contain a word no reader expects. Checking for the unset case and substituting a blank is the fix.

prompt: A literal is opened with a single quote and contains an apostrophe partway through. Where does the literal end?
optionA: At the closing quote at the end of the line
optionB: At the apostrophe, since it matches the opening quote
optionC: At the end of the line, wherever that falls
optionD: It does not end, and the file is truncated
correctAnswerText: At the apostrophe, since it matches the opening quote
explanation: The apostrophe is indistinguishable from a closing quote, so the literal ends there. Everything after it is read as something else entirely.

prompt: A developer writes a sentence containing an apostrophe inside single quotes and the file will not run. The apostrophe matches the opening quote and ends the literal early. What are the two ways to fix it?
optionA: Remove the apostrophe, or shorten the sentence
optionB: Use double quotes, or move the sentence to its own line
optionC: Escape the apostrophe, or remove the surrounding quotes
optionD: Use double quotes around the whole sentence, or escape the apostrophe
correctAnswerText: Use double quotes around the whole sentence, or escape the apostrophe
explanation: Either choosing a quote form the text does not contain, or escaping the offending character, resolves it. Removing the apostrophe changes the text rather than fixing the code.

prompt: A path written with single backslashes behaves wrongly, and inspecting it shows a line break where a backslash and the letter n were written. What happened?
optionA: That pair formed an escape sequence and became a line break
optionB: The path was truncated at the backslash
optionC: The backslash was removed entirely
optionD: The whole path was converted to a different form
correctAnswerText: That pair formed an escape sequence and became a line break
explanation: Only that pair was converted; the rest of the path is as written. A raw literal or doubled backslashes would have kept it intact.

prompt: Two paths written the same way behave differently: one works and one does not. Only some backslash-and-letter pairs form an escape sequence, and the two paths use different letters after their backslashes. Why do they differ?
optionA: One path is longer than the other
optionB: One path points at a file that does not exist
optionC: One path happens to contain a pair that forms an escape and the other does not
optionD: The two were written with different quote forms
correctAnswerText: One path happens to contain a pair that forms an escape and the other does not
explanation: The behaviour depends on which letters follow the backslashes, which varies from path to path. That unevenness is why the fault appears to come and go.

prompt: A value is displayed rounded to two decimal places and then used in a later calculation. Which value does the calculation use?
optionA: The rounded value that was displayed
optionB: The original unrounded value
optionC: Whichever was used most recently
optionD: An average of the two
correctAnswerText: The original unrounded value
explanation: Formatting produces text and leaves the value untouched. Rounding the value itself is a separate operation.

prompt: Three amounts are each displayed rounded to two decimal places, and their total is computed from the unrounded values and displayed the same way. A reader adds the three displayed figures and gets a different answer. The three displayed figures are rounded individually while the total is computed from the unrounded values. Why do they disagree?
optionA: One of the three figures was displayed incorrectly
optionB: The total was computed from the wrong values
optionC: The rounding was applied twice to the total
optionD: The rounding of each figure is lost from the total, which was computed before any rounding
correctAnswerText: The rounding of each figure is lost from the total, which was computed before any rounding
explanation: Everything here is correct and the displayed figures cannot be expected to add up. Rounding each value before summing is what makes the report internally consistent.

prompt: A team fixes a report that did not add up by rounding each value before summing. An auditor objects that the total is now wrong. Rounding before summing makes the report add up and moves the total away from the exact figure. Who is right?
optionA: Both; the report is now internally consistent and its total no longer matches the exact figure
optionB: The team; a report that adds up is correct
optionC: The auditor; the total must always be exact
optionD: Neither; the two totals are identical
correctAnswerText: Both; the report is now internally consistent and its total no longer matches the exact figure
explanation: The two requirements genuinely conflict and only one can be satisfied. Which matters depends on whether the report is read by people adding columns or fed into something needing the exact figure.

prompt: A value is stored, displayed rounded, read back from the display by another system, and stored again. The value stored the second time came from the rounded text rather than from the original value. What has happened to the precision?
optionA: Nothing; formatting never changes a value
optionB: It is recoverable from the original store
optionC: It has been lost permanently, since the rounding became the stored value
optionD: It is halved with each round trip
correctAnswerText: It has been lost permanently, since the rounding became the stored value
explanation: Formatting leaves the value alone right up until the formatted text is read back as data. That round trip is where display rounding becomes real.

prompt: A developer displays a value with no format at all and finds it shows many more decimal places than expected. Displaying without a format writes out the value as it is actually held rather than as it was typed. What does that reveal?
optionA: A fault in the display
optionB: What the value actually holds, which differs from what was typed in
optionC: That the value has been corrupted
optionD: That a format is required for every value
correctAnswerText: What the value actually holds, which differs from what was typed in
explanation: The unformatted display is the honest one and the surprise is about how such values are stored. A format hides the difference rather than removing it.

prompt: A piece of text contains several single quotes and no double quotes. The text contains single quotes and no double quotes, and choosing the form the text avoids removes the need to escape anything. Which form fits?
optionA: Single quotes, with each internal quote escaped
optionB: Single quotes, with the internal quotes removed
optionC: Triple single quotes, with each internal quote escaped
optionD: Double quotes, with nothing escaped
correctAnswerText: Double quotes, with nothing escaped
explanation: Choosing the form the text does not contain is the simplest route and needs no escaping. Escaping works and produces a harder literal to read.

prompt: A piece of text is a Windows path ending in a backslash. A developer proposes a raw literal to avoid escaping. A raw literal cannot end in a single backslash, because that backslash would escape the closing quote. What follows?
optionA: A raw literal will not work here, so the backslashes must be doubled in an ordinary literal
optionB: A raw literal works and is the right choice
optionC: The path cannot be written in any form
optionD: A triple-quoted raw literal solves it
correctAnswerText: A raw literal will not work here, so the backslashes must be doubled in an ordinary literal
explanation: This is the one thing a raw literal cannot express, and it is exactly the case paths run into. Doubling the backslashes in an ordinary literal is the way out.

prompt: A message spans four lines and must preserve the line breaks. A developer proposes a triple-quoted literal placed inside a deeply indented block. A triple-quoted literal keeps the indentation of the lines it contains, and the block is deeply indented. What should they consider?
optionA: Nothing; indentation is stripped automatically
optionB: That triple quotes cannot be used inside an indented block
optionC: That the indentation will become part of the text and has to be removed or avoided
optionD: That the line breaks will be lost
correctAnswerText: That the indentation will become part of the text and has to be removed or avoided
explanation: The form is right for the requirement and brings the indentation with it. Dedenting afterwards, or writing the literal unindented, both address it.

prompt: A message is built from a fixed sentence and one value. A developer can use interpolation or join the parts with an operator. The value is a number and joining with an operator requires converting it to text first, while interpolation writes it out directly. Which fits?
optionA: Joining, since it is more explicit
optionB: Interpolation, since it writes the value out without a separate conversion
optionC: Joining, since interpolation is slower
optionD: Either; the two require the same amount of code
correctAnswerText: Interpolation, since it writes the value out without a separate conversion
explanation: Joining a number to text without converting it is an error, so the operator route carries an extra step. Both produce identical text once that step is taken.

prompt: A long piece of text must be written across several source lines without introducing line breaks into the value. Adjacent quoted pieces join with nothing between them, and a triple-quoted literal keeps every line break. Which form fits?
optionA: A triple-quoted literal spanning the lines
optionB: A triple-quoted raw literal spanning the lines
optionC: One very long line, since no other form works
optionD: Several adjacent quoted pieces, one per source line
correctAnswerText: Several adjacent quoted pieces, one per source line
explanation: Adjacency joins the pieces and the source line breaks are not part of any literal. A triple-quoted form would put every one of those breaks into the value.

prompt: A language is documented as follows: text is written between backticks; a backslash before any character produces that character literally; there is no interpolation. A literal is written containing a backslash followed by the letter n. The rules state that a backslash produces the following character literally, and there is no special meaning for any letter. What does the literal contain?
optionA: The letter n
optionB: A line break
optionC: A backslash and the letter n
optionD: Nothing; the escape is invalid
correctAnswerText: The letter n
explanation: These rules differ from the ones this skill has been using, and the stated rules are what govern. Assuming a line break would be importing a convention the description rules out.

prompt: A configuration format is documented as treating every value as literal text with no escape processing whatsoever. A developer writes a path containing backslashes into it. No escape processing occurs, so every character stands for itself. What does the value contain?
optionA: The path with escape sequences converted
optionB: The path with backslashes doubled
optionC: Exactly the characters written, backslashes included
optionD: An error, since backslashes must be escaped
correctAnswerText: Exactly the characters written, backslashes included
explanation: A format with no escape processing behaves like a raw literal everywhere. That also means there is no way to write a character the format uses structurally.

prompt: A template system is documented as substituting anything between double braces and leaving single braces alone. A developer writes a message containing a literal double brace they do not want substituted. Double braces are always substituted and the documentation describes no way to escape them. What follows?
optionA: Single braces should be used instead, which produce the same output
optionB: The message cannot express a literal double brace, so the format has to be extended or avoided
optionC: The double brace will be left alone since no name follows it
optionD: The system will report an error and leave the text unchanged
correctAnswerText: The message cannot express a literal double brace, so the format has to be extended or avoided
explanation: A format that reserves a sequence and offers no escape cannot express that sequence. Recognising the gap is the point; working around it is a separate decision.

prompt: A team must choose between a message format that substitutes values automatically and one that requires every value to be inserted explicitly. Messages sometimes contain characters the substituting format treats as structural. A format that substitutes automatically will act on those characters wherever they appear in the message. Which fits messages containing arbitrary user text?
optionA: The substituting form, since it is more convenient
optionB: The substituting form, since users rarely type such characters
optionC: Either, since both produce the same messages
optionD: The explicit form, since arbitrary text will otherwise collide with the structural characters
correctAnswerText: The explicit form, since arbitrary text will otherwise collide with the structural characters
explanation: Automatic substitution is convenient right up until the content contains what the format reserves. Arbitrary user text is precisely the case where that stops being rare.
